meta.title: Who really said "Nobody is more inferior than those who insist on being equal"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. This anti-egalitarian one-liner appears in none of Nietzsche’s works — it surfaces in a modern mock interview, wedged between two real lines from Beyond Good and Evil.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nobody is more inferior than those who insist on being equal'?
meta.ogDescription: Nietzsche never wrote this. The wording traces to a fictional web ‘interview,’ slipped between two genuine lines from Beyond Good and Evil §212.

answer.label: Not Nietzsche’s words — an unsourced modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The anti-egalitarian sentiment is broadly Nietzschean, but this exact sentence is found in none of his books, letters, or notebooks. Wikiquote lists it under ‘Disputed’ ↗, noting no citation is ever given; the only source that puts it in Nietzsche’s mouth is a modern fictional ‘interview’ that spliced the line between two real passages of Beyond Good and Evil.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: A fictional ‘3:16’ interview by Richard Marshall

source.excerpt: “The philosopher has to be the bad conscience of his age. … nobody is more inferior than those who insist on being equal. He shall be the greatest who can be the most solitary, the most concealed, the most divergent, the one beyond good and evil, the master of his virtues…”
trail: Wikiquote’s Nietzsche page ↗ files the line under Disputed, noting “no citation is ever given” and that the sole source is a mock interview by Richard Marshall.
In that fictional ‘3:16’ interview ↗, the sentence is wedged between two real lines from Beyond Good and Evil §212 — which is how quote-harvesters mistook it for Nietzsche.
A reading of Beyond Good and Evil §212 ↗ confirms the surrounding phrases are genuine but the ‘equal’ line is absent.
Aggregators like AZQuotes ↗ and Goodreads ↗ repeat it with no work, page, or edition.
source.excerptNote: From Richard Marshall’s fictional interview. The first and third sentences are genuine Nietzsche (Beyond Good and Evil §212); the middle sentence — the ‘quote’ — is the inserted line that does not appear in §212 or anywhere else in Nietzsche.
source.rightsNote: No public-domain or copyright status can be asserted, because the wording is not from any identified Nietzsche work. It appears to be a modern paraphrase whose earliest traceable appearance is Richard Marshall’s fictional web interview; the genuine surrounding lines are from Beyond Good and Evil (1886, long in the public domain), but this specific sentence is not among them.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: Who was Friedrich Nietzsche?
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German philosopher and philologist whose works — Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil, On the Genealogy of Morality — attacked egalitarian and ‘herd’ morality and championed hierarchy, self-overcoming, and the individual. Because he genuinely was anti-egalitarian, punchy modern one-liners on ‘equality’ are easily pinned on him without a source. His aphoristic, densely argued style rarely reduces to a tidy epigram like this one.

cite.sourceCitation: No source in Nietzsche’s works. Earliest documented appearance: Richard Marshall, “Exclusive 3:16 Interview with Friedrich Nietzsche” (3:16 AM Magazine, fictional interview), where the line is interpolated among genuine passages of Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil (1886), §212.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone thinks Nietzsche said it
misattribution.intro: The line rides on Nietzsche’s real reputation as an enemy of ‘equality’ — but no book, letter, or notebook of his contains it. Its trail leads to a modern fictional interview, not to Nietzsche.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ places it under ‘Disputed,’ observing that “no citation is ever given” and that the only source attributing it to Nietzsche is a mock interview.
In this imagined Q&A ↗, the sentence appears between two genuine lines from Beyond Good and Evil §212 — so extractors lifted it as if it were Nietzsche’s own.

items.who: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil
items.why: The framing phrases — ‘the bad conscience of his age’ and ‘he shall be the greatest who can be the most solitary’ — are authentic §212 ↗, but the ‘insist on being equal’ sentence is not there.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: Nietzsche never wrote this sentence. It is an unsourced modern paraphrase whose earliest home is a fictional interview ↗ — and Wikiquote ↗ flags it as disputed.

context.heading: The sentiment is his; the sentence isn’t
lead: Nietzsche really did scorn the demand for equality — he saw the leveling drive of ‘herd morality’ as hostile to greatness and self-overcoming. That is exactly why a slogan like this sticks to him so easily: it sounds right.

But sounding Nietzschean is not the same as being Nietzsche. His actual prose argues; it rarely delivers a bumper-sticker. This tidy inversion — the equality-seekers are the truly inferior ones — is the shape a meme takes, not the shape of §212, and its documented trail begins in a modern web piece that was openly fictional.
context.detailsSummary: How a real passage became a fake quote
detailsBody: A writer builds a fictional interview by stringing together genuine Nietzsche lines. To make the ‘answer’ flow, an extra sentence is added in his voice. Readers copy the vivid middle sentence, drop the fictional frame, and a ‘Nietzsche quote’ is born — complete with the authority of the real lines that once surrounded it.
context.pull: The idea is Nietzschean. The sentence is not Nietzsche.
